title: Where they fell short
hookLine: the Stoics lived with slavery and empire, and admiring them doesn't mean agreeing with everything

lines: A HERO WHO TURNED OUT TO BE A PERSON.
cards: Everybody has had a hero who turned out to be a person. A coach, a grandparent, a musician whose songs got you through a hard year, and then one day you learn something about them that doesn't fit.
What do you do with that? Throw them out entirely? Pretend you didn't hear it?
There's a third way. This path has quoted the Stoics for most of a year, so i owe it to them, and to you, to try it here.

teach.h: ONE REASON, AND A SLAVE SOCIETY.
teach.b: Start with slavery. The Stoics said all humans share the same reason, that we're citizens of one world, that a slave's mind is as free as an emperor's.
And they lived in a society built on slavery and never, as far as we know, called for ending it.

Seneca wrote a well-known letter telling his friend to treat enslaved people as human beings: eat with them, speak kindly, remember that fortune could swap your places. That's real, and more than many Romans said.
But Seneca himself owned many people, and the letter asks for kinder masters, not for no masters.
Then wealth and power. Seneca was enormously rich while writing about the simple life, and he served as adviser to Nero.
When Nero had his own mother killed, the historian Tacitus reports that Seneca was believed to have written the letter explaining it to the Senate.
Marcus Aurelius spent much of his reign at war, and Christians were put to death in parts of the empire while he ruled; historians still debate how much he knew or directed.

teach.h: KEEP WHAT HOLDS, NAME WHAT DOESN'T.
teach.b: So what do we do? The Stoics hand us the tool themselves. Epictetus said no one is a finished sage; everyone is making progress, or not.

They never claimed to be perfect. Admiring them honestly means keeping the teaching that holds, the dichotomy of control, the circles, the citadel, and naming plainly where they didn't live up to their own best ideas.
Which raises an uncomfortable question: what will people three hundred years from now say we couldn't see?

how: Many modern readers of the Stoics keep their practical teachings while openly acknowledging the Stoics' acceptance of slavery and their entanglement with wealth and imperial power.

as far as we know, none called for abolition; Seneca asked for humane treatment.

games.q: you learn that a thinker you admire accepted something terrible in his time. what does honest admiration do?
o: keep what holds, and name what doesn't.
games.why: the Stoics called themselves people making progress; we can keep the teaching and say plainly where they fell short.

practice: Wonder about our own time: what do almost all of us accept, the way Romans accepted slavery, that people later might find hard to believe? Let one candidate come up; it doesn't need to be a perfect answer.
Hold it without defending yourself or beating yourself up, and only notice.

wordCard.voice: Seneca, the Stoic who taught equality while owning slaves and advising Nero: admire the Stoics honestly, not blindly.

orig.note: Latin, Seneca Letter 47: they are slaves; no, they are human beings.

carryVoice: Your line: honest admiration. The teaching can hold even where the teachers fell short. See you tomorrow.
